summary: This informational memo documents MAPOS 16, a multiple access protocol that carries datagrams in HDLC frames with 16-bit addressing over SONET/SDH.

plainLanguage.summary: MAPOS lets several computers share one optical line that was built for just two ends. RFC 2175 describes a version of MAPOS with a longer address field, so a shared line can hold far more devices.

questions: what is the mapos 16 frame format
how are ip multicast addresses mapped in mapos 16
subtitle: MAPOS with a 16-bit address field, so a shared SONET/SDH network can hold far more nodes.

tldr.problem: MAPOS version 1 keeps its frames compatible with conventional PPP, and so has a narrow 8-bit address field, which limits how many nodes can share a SONET/SDH network.
tldr.mechanism: MAPOS 16 uses HDLC-like framing with a 16-bit address field and drops the control field to keep the header 32-bit aligned. The 16-bit addresses sit in the low bits of the existing 32-bit address fields of the other MAPOS protocols.
tldr.outcome: The wider address space leaves the MAPOS protocol family, ARP, UNARP, NSP and SSP, essentially unchanged. The memo is Informational, and its authors say it is not a standards track document.

today: RFC 2175 is an Informational memo, and the metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The authors say it is not a standards track document, so it documents MAPOS 16 rather than defining a standard.

sections.title: MAPOS and the Move to 16 Bits
sections.content:
MAPOS is a multiple access protocol for the transmission of High-level Data Link Control frames over SONET/SDH. It provides multiple access capability on SONET/SDH, which is an inherently point-to-point link.

MAPOS version 1 focuses on frame format compatibility with conventional PPP, and that results in its narrow 8-bit address field. MAPOS 16 has a 16-bit address space instead, and the authors say this offers a significantly wide address space. The primary difference between the two is that one change.

The authors also say plainly what kind of document this is. It is not the product of an IETF working group and not a standards track document, so it has not necessarily benefited from the widespread and in-depth community review that standards track documents receive. The memo documents MAPOS 16 for transmitting network protocol datagrams encapsulated in HDLC frames with 16-bit addressing over SONET/SDH, describes the header format and the 16-bit address format, and explains that 16-bit addressing has minimal influence on the conventional MAPOS protocol family such as the Node-Switch Protocol and the Switch-Switch Protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: MAPOS lets many computers share one fibre line instead of just two. The new version simply gives each of them a longer address.

sections.title: The MAPOS 16 Frame
sections.content:
Like MAPOS version 1, MAPOS 16 framing is based on the HDLC-like framing used in PPP-over-SONET/SDH, described in RFC 1662. The address field is extended to 16 bits, and the control field present in MAPOS version 1 is omitted to maintain the 32-bit alignment of the header. Logical Link Control and SNAP are not used. The fields are transmitted from left to right.

The flag is used for frame synchronisation. Each frame begins and ends with the flag sequence 01111110, which is 0x7E. If a frame immediately follows another, one flag sequence may be treated as the end of the preceding frame and the beginning of the following one, and when the line is idle the flag sequence is transmitted continuously.

The address field contains the destination HDLC address, and a frame is forwarded by a switch based on this field. The protocol field indicates the protocol the datagram in the information field belongs to; it conforms to the ISO 3309 extension mechanism, and its value may be obtained from the most recent Assigned Numbers and MAPOS Version 1 Assigned Numbers. The information field contains that datagram, and its length may vary but shall not exceed 65,280 octets, which is 64K minus 256. The frame check sequence is 16 bits long by default, and 32 bits may be used instead. It is calculated over all bits of the address, protocol and information fields prior to escape conversions, and the least significant octet of the result is transmitted first.

A sending station must continuously transmit the flag sequence as inter-frame fill after the FCS field, and the receiving station must silently discard those flags. When an under-run occurs during DMA in the sending station, it must abort the frame transfer and continuously send the flag sequence to indicate the error.

MAPOS 16 uses the same octet stuffing procedure as MAPOS version 1. Since SONET/SDH provides transparency, the Async-Control-Character-Map is not used. Each HDLC frame is separated from another by one or more flag sequences, and an escape sequence is defined to escape the flag sequence and itself. Before sending the frame, but after the FCS computation, every occurrence of 01111110 other than the flags is converted to 01111101 01011110, and the sequence 01111101 is converted to 01111101 01011101. On receiving a frame, the conversion is reversed before the FCS is computed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is wrapped like a parcel: a start marker, an address, a note saying what is inside, the contents, a check number, and an end marker. Data that happens to look like the start marker is disguised, and the receiver removes the disguise.

sections.title: The 16-Bit Address Field
sections.content:
The least significant bit of the first byte of the address field indicates the continuation of the field and must always be 0, and the least significant bit of the second byte indicates the end of the field and must always be 1. These are the two EA bits. The most significant bit of the first byte says whether the frame is unicast or multicast: a value of 0 means unicast, with the remaining thirteen bits giving the destination node address including the two EA bits, and a value of 1 means multicast, with the remaining thirteen bits giving the group address.

The address 0xFEFF means that the frame is a broadcast frame. The address 0x0001 is reserved to identify the control processor inside a switch. Frames with an invalid address should be silently discarded.

Section 5 covers IP multicast. When transmitting IP multicast, the thirteen bits of the HDLC address must contain the lowest-order thirteen bits of the IP multicast group address. An exception arises when those thirteen bits are either all zeros or all ones, in which case the address 1111 1110 1111 1101 should be used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The address has a first bit that says whether the message is for one house or for a whole group, and the remaining bits are the house or group number. Two addresses are reserved, one for broadcast and one for the switch's own control processor.

sections.title: Effect on the MAPOS Protocol Family
sections.content:
All of the MAPOS protocol family, ARP, UNARP, NSP and SSP, use a 32-bit address field for the 8-bit MAPOS address, so the 16-bit addressing has no influence on them. Each protocol only has to place a 16-bit address in the least significant place in its 32-bit address field.

For MAPOS ARP and UNARP, the 16-bit addresses are placed in the least significant places of the 32-bit sender and target HDLC addresses. For NSP, in an address assignment packet a 16-bit address is placed in the least significant bytes of the 32-bit address field and the rest of the field is padded with zeros. For SSP, in a route entry of an SSP packet the 16-bit MAPOS address is placed in the least significant bytes of the 32-bit address field.
sections.plainLanguage: The other MAPOS protocols already had room for a longer number, so the new address simply slides into the end of the field they already use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo says only that security issues are not discussed in it. Anyone deploying MAPOS 16 would need to look elsewhere for guidance, since this RFC gives none.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo does not say anything about keeping the line safe from snoopers.

viz.caption: THE SPECIAL CASES IN THE ADDRESS FIELD

items.title: Broadcast
items.text: The address 0xFEFF means the frame is for everyone.

items.title: Control processor
items.text: The address 0x0001 is reserved for the control processor inside a switch.

items.title: Invalid addresses
items.text: Frames with an invalid address should be silently discarded.

items.title: IP multicast
items.text: The thirteen bits hold the lowest-order thirteen bits of the IP multicast group address.

items.title: All zeros or all ones
items.text: In that case the address 1111 1110 1111 1101 is used instead.
